'''Mavis Bowler Carroll''' (October 12, 1917 – March 7, 2009){{r|obit}} was an American [[statistician]] who pioneered the industrial use of statistics in her work at [[General Foods]].{{r|hoerl}}

Carroll finished high school at age 16 and attended the [[New Jersey College for Women]] on a scholarship. She played on the school basketball team, and earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics there in 1938. She worked as a [[code breaker]] during [[World War II]]{{r|obit}} and at the Squibb Institute for Medical Research in [[New Brunswick, New Jersey]] in the early 1950s.{{r|squibb}}

Later, she worked at the [[General Foods]] Research Center, where she became Section Head in 1958{{r|nn}} and, by the 1960s, the head of their division of mathematical and statistical services.{{r|tea}} Her work at General Foods included the design and analysis of [[Blind taste test|taste tests]], with each variation of a food product typically being tested by a panel of 50 tasters (evenly split by gender) who rated the foods on a scale of +3 to &minus;3. In order to keep the total number of tasters manageable, a careful [[design of experiments]] was needed to control the number of different food variations to be tested.{{r|counting}}

Carroll was secretary of the American Society for Testing and Materials for 1960 to 1962.{{r|astm}}
In 1971, Carroll was elected as a [[Fellow of the American Statistical Association]].{{r|fasa}}

Carroll died of pneumonia on March 7, 2009, in [[Wilmington, North Carolina]].{{r|obit}}
